mainTopic: The range of a שבועת ביטוי: oaths about others, about things with no substance, and about the past
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion of why a certain משנה, which lists prohibitions for one act of eating, leaves out a שבועה. The final answer is that the list only counts prohibitions on physical things, while a שבועה can apply even to sleeping. Then a new משנה teaches that a שבועת ביטוי covers matters of oneself or others, and things with or without substance, like sleeping or throwing a pebble into the sea. רבי ישמעאל limits liability to oaths about the future, and רבי עקיבא argues that past oaths count too. The גמרא brings a ברייתא: a נדר takes effect on a מצוה matter, while a שבועה takes effect on things with no substance. It then explains the משנה's examples. 'I will give' means a gift to a rich person, not צדקה. 'I will not sleep' works only if he did not say 'three days'. Finally, רב and שמואל argue about an oath that someone else threw a stone. The גמרא shows that both follow רבי עקיבא and disagree about how far his view reaches. A new comparison begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The rule was only about חטאות
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge about הקדש: when we said the list only includes כרת sins, we meant only the חטאות in the list.
steps.simpleTranslation: We were speaking about the חטאת offerings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends its earlier answer by saying the 'only כרת' rule was meant only for the חטאות in the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא said the משנה only lists sins that carry כרת, and it was challenged because the משנה also lists an אשם for הקדש, which has no כרת. The answer narrows the rule: the 'only כרת' idea applies to the חטאות. The אשם of הקדש is a separate kind of קרבן and does not break the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: A sin-offering brought for doing a כרת sin by accident
Spiritual cutting off, the punishment for certain sins done on purpose

phrases.english: We are speaking about sin-offerings.
phrases.notes: He means the 'only כרת sins' rule was about the חטאות in the list, not the אשם for הקדש.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers a challenge from the previous part of the daf (the אשם of הקדש has no כרת).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the scope of the original rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule 'the משנה only lists כרת sins' seemed to cover every קרבן in the list, including the אשם.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule only covers the חטאות; the אשם for הקדש is a separate item, so the rule still holds and a שבועה is still left out.

steps.title: רבינא: the list only includes prohibitions on food
steps.stepSummary: רבינא gives a different reason the שבועה is left out: the משנה only lists prohibitions that apply to food, while a שבועה can apply to non-food items too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: When the תנא teaches the list, he includes things that apply to items that are food. A שבועה, which can also apply to items that are not food, he does not teach.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא offers a new, separate answer to why the משנה does not list a שבועה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is about one act of eating, so רבינא says it only lists prohibitions that by nature are about food. A שבועה is a general tool that can be placed on anything, food or not. So it does not belong in a list of food prohibitions.

keyTerms.meaning: Something fit to be eaten, food

phrases.english: Ravina said:
When he teaches, it is things that apply
to items that are edible;
an oath, which applies to items
that are not edible,
he does not teach.
phrases.notes: Since a שבועה can also work on things that are not food, it does not fit this list.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer instead of the 'only כרת' approach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defining the category of the list
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a שבועה not to eat can make someone liable for eating, it seems the משנה should have counted it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה only lists prohibitions that by nature apply to food, and a שבועה is broader than that.

steps.title: But הקדש applies to wood and stones
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבינא: הקדש is in the list, yet it also applies to things that are not food, like wood and stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there is הקדש, which also applies to wood and stones!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבינא's answer with an example from the משנה's own list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא said the list only includes prohibitions that apply to food. But the משנה lists the prohibition of using הקדש, and something can become הקדש even if it is wood or stone. So 'food only' cannot be the reason a שבועה is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: But look at / but there is
Property set aside for the בית המקדש, which may not be used for personal benefit

phrases.english: But there is consecrated property,
which also applies to wood and stones!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבינא's answer from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's claim that the משנה only lists prohibitions that apply to food
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: הקדש is listed in the משנה even though it also applies to non-food items, so 'food only' is not the rule of the list.

steps.title: The list includes only prohibitions on physical things
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא revises רבינא's answer: the משנה lists prohibitions that apply to physical, touchable things, but a שבועה can even apply to actions like sleeping.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, when he teaches, it is things that apply to items that have physical substance. A שבועה, which can apply to things that have no physical substance, such as 'that I will sleep' or 'that I will not sleep', he does not teach.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes רבינא's answer so it can handle the challenge from הקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The line is moved from 'food' to 'physical things'. הקדש, even wood and stones, is still a physical object, so it fits the list. A שבועה can be about an action with no physical object at all, like sleeping, so it is a different kind of prohibition and is left out.

keyTerms.meaning: Physical substance, something you can touch

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה only counts prohibitions on physical things. A שבועה is left out because it can even be about actions with no object, like sleeping.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean a שבועה not to eat fails to take effect on food. It only explains why this list does not count it, since a שבועה is a broader kind of prohibition.

phrases.english: Rather, when he teaches,

phrases.aramaic: מִידֵּי דְּחָיֵיל אַמִּידֵּי דְּאִית בֵּהּ מְשָׁשָׁא;
phrases.english: it is things that apply to items that have substance;
phrases.notes: Literally 'something you can feel', meaning a real, physical object.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁבוּעָה דְּחָיְילָא אַמִּידֵּי דְּלֵית בֵּיהּ מְשָׁשָׁא,
phrases.english: an oath, which applies to matters that have no substance,
such as 'that I will sleep' and 'that I will not sleep',
he does not teach.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 3 by reworking רבינא's answer from step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The list was thought to be defined by food, which הקדש on wood and stones did not fit.
steps.terutzMaskana: The list is defined by physical objects. הקדש fits, but a שבועה, which can apply to actions like sleeping, does not.

steps.title: The oath applies to oneself, to others, and to things with or without substance
steps.stepSummary: The משנה states the general rule: a שבועת ביטוי can be about matters that concern oneself or others, and about things with substance or without substance.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: It does not matter whether the oath is about your own matters or about other people's matters. It also does not matter whether it is about something that has physical substance or something that has none.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins and sets out a broad rule about which oaths count as a שבועת ביטוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה widens the scope of the oath in two ways. First, it covers oaths involving other people, not just yourself. Second, it covers oaths about things you cannot touch, not only physical objects.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for מַתְנִיתִין, 'our משנה'. It marks the start of a new משנה.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
Both matters that concern oneself
and matters that concern others,
and both matters that have substance
and matters that have no substance.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶחָד דְּבָרִים שֶׁל עַצְמוֹ וְאֶחָד דְּבָרִים שֶׁל אֲחֵרִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the previous discussion of why שבועה was left out of an earlier list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שבועת ביטוי applies to one's own matters and to others' matters, and to things with or without physical substance.

steps.title: Examples of oaths involving another person
steps.stepSummary: The משנה asks 'How so?' and gives the first examples: oaths about giving or not giving something to a certain person, in the future and in the past.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? For example, someone says: 'I swear I will give this to so-and-so,' or 'I swear I will not give it.' Or: 'I swear I gave it,' or 'I swear I did not give it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts explaining its general rule with real examples. These first ones show oaths that involve another person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving to 'so-and-so' illustrates 'matters of others', since the oath affects another person. Each example comes in four forms: a future yes, a future no, a past yes, and a past no.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? It introduces examples that explain a rule.

phrases.english: How so?
He said: "On my oath, I will give to so-and-so"
or: "that I will not give";
"that I gave" or "that I did not give";

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיצַד? אָמַר שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁאֶתֵּן לְאִישׁ פְּלוֹנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates the rule from step 5 about oaths that concern others.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath to give or not give something to another person, or that one did or did not give it, counts as a שבועת ביטוי.

steps.title: Examples of oaths about things with no substance: sleeping and throwing a pebble
steps.stepSummary: The משנה gives examples of oaths about things with no physical substance: sleeping, and throwing a pebble into the sea, each in the future and in the past.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or: 'I swear I will sleep,' or 'I will not sleep'; 'I swear I slept,' or 'I did not sleep.' Or: 'I swear I will throw a pebble into the sea,' or 'I will not throw it'; 'I swear I threw it,' or 'I did not throw it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues its examples. These show oaths about actions that have no physical substance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sleeping is an action, not an object, so it illustrates 'things with no substance'. Throwing a pebble into the sea is a pointless act that helps no one. The משנה still counts both as a שבועת ביטוי. This fits Step 4, where the גמרא said a שבועה can apply even to sleeping.

phrases.english: "that I will sleep" or "that I will not sleep";
"that I slept" or "that I did not sleep";
"that I will throw a pebble into the sea" or "that I will not throw";
"that I threw" or "that I did not throw."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the examples, now for oaths about things with no physical substance.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Oaths about intangible actions like sleeping or throwing a pebble into the sea, in the future or the past, count as a שבועת ביטוי.
steps.whatToRemember: According to the first opinion in the משנה, a שבועת ביטוי covers oaths about oneself or others, about things with or without substance, and about the future or the past.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל: liability only for oaths about the future
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל disagrees and says a person is liable only for an oath about the future, because the פסוק says 'to do bad or to do good'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל says: A person is liable only for an oath about the future, as the פסוק says: 'to do bad or to do good.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion appears in the משנה. רבי ישמעאל limits the oath to future actions only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'לְהָרַע אוֹ לְהֵיטִיב' describe something a person is going to do. So רבי ישמעאל reads the פסוק as covering only oaths about the future. That would exclude the past examples above, like 'I gave' or 'I slept'.

keyTerms.meaning: The future; what is yet to come
To do bad or to do good; words from the פסוק about oaths

steps.confusionAlert: רבי ישמעאל is not rejecting the whole list. He only removes the past-tense examples, such as 'I gave' or 'I slept'. The future-tense oaths still count according to him.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael says:

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא עַל הֶעָתִיד לָבֹא,
phrases.english: He is liable only for the future,
as it is said: "to do bad or to do good."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹמֵר: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא עַל הֶעָתִיד לָבֹא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion, which included past-tense oaths.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי ישמעאל, a person is liable for a שבועת ביטוי only when the oath is about the future.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the main disagreement of the משנה: does a שבועת ביטוי include oaths about the past, or only oaths about the future?

steps.title: רבי עקיבא challenges: what about oaths that are neither bad nor good?
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא argues that if we follow the exact words 'to do bad or to do good,' we lose oaths about things that are neither bad nor good.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: If so, the פסוק only teaches me about things that involve doing bad or doing good. Where do we learn about things that are neither bad nor good?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא attacks רבי ישמעאל's reasoning from the words 'to do bad or to do good.' He points out that this reasoning would leave out many oaths that everyone agrees count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל limited liability to the future because of the words 'להרע או להיטיב.' רבי עקיבא answers: if you read those words strictly, an oath like 'I will throw a pebble into the sea' should not count, because it is neither bad nor good. Yet both of them agree such an oath counts. So the strict reading cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: if your reasoning is correct
Doing bad and doing good (from the פסוק 'לְהָרַע אוֹ לְהֵיטִיב')
From where do we know it?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: אִם כֵּן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to him: If so,
I have only matters
that involve doing bad and doing good;

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶן הֲרָעָה וַהֲטָבָה מִנַּיִן?
phrases.english: matters that do not involve doing bad and doing good, from where do we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: אִם כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds directly to רבי ישמעאל's derivation in Step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's strict reading of 'להרע או להיטיב' as limiting liability
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A strict reading would also exclude neutral oaths like throwing a pebble, which are clearly included.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל answers: the פסוק includes them
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל replies that neutral oaths are learned from an extra inclusion in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We learn it from an inclusion in the פסוק.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל defends himself. He says the neutral cases are not left out, because the פסוק has extra wording that adds them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל agrees the words 'bad or good' alone would not cover neutral oaths. But he says the פסוק widens itself to include them. He still keeps his limit to oaths about the future.

keyTerms.meaning: An inclusion of the פסוק: extra wording that widens the law to more cases

phrases.english: He said to him: From the inclusion of the verse.
phrases.notes: Here 'he' is רבי ישמעאל answering רבי עקיבא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי עקיבא's challenge in Step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Source answer: a different part of the פסוק adds the missing cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Neutral oaths would be excluded, since they are neither bad nor good.
steps.terutzMaskana: Neutral oaths are included through an inclusion in the פסוק, while the future-only limit stays.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא's comeback: then the past is included too
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers that if the פסוק can be widened for neutral oaths, it can also be widened for oaths about the past.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If the פסוק includes for this, then the פסוק includes for that!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא turns רבי ישמעאל's own answer against him. This ends the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we stop reading 'להרע או להיטיב' strictly and let the פסוק widen itself, nothing is left to exclude the past. The same widening that adds neutral oaths should add oaths about the past.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי ישמעאל: liable only for oaths about the future, based on 'to do bad or to do good.' רבי עקיבא: once the פסוק is widened anyway, oaths about the past are included too.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אִם רִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב לְכָךְ,
phrases.english: He said to him: If the verse included for this,
phrases.notes: 'This' means oaths about things that are neither bad nor good.

phrases.english: the verse included for that!
phrases.notes: 'That' means oaths about the past, which רבי ישמעאל wanted to leave out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אִם רִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב לְכָךְ, רִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב לְכָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי ישמעאל's answer from Step 10 by applying its own logic to the past.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's use of רִיבּוּי while still excluding oaths about the past
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once you widen the פסוק, you cannot widen it for one case and refuse to widen it for the other.

steps.title: A ברייתא: each of vows and oaths has its own stringency; vows apply even to a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with a ברייתא. Vows and oaths each have a stringency, and the first is that a נדר takes effect even on a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא. The Rabbis taught: There is a stringency in vows over oaths, and a stringency in oaths over vows. The stringency in vows is that vows take effect on a מצוה matter just like on an optional matter, which is not so with oaths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts by quoting a ברייתא that compares נדרים and שבועות. It begins with the area where a נדר is stronger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither one is simply stronger: each has an advantage. A נדר takes effect even on something connected to a מצוה, the same as on an optional matter. A שבועה does not take effect on a מצוה matter.

keyTerms.meaning: A stringency: a way one is stricter than the other
An optional matter, neither required nor forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up נדר and שבועה. They are two different tools, and this ברייתא is pointing out how they differ.

phrases.english: GEMARA. The Rabbis taught:
There is a stringency in vows over oaths,
and a stringency in oaths over vows.
The stringency in vows: that vows take effect
on a matter of a מצוה just like on an optional matter,
which is not so with oaths.
phrases.notes: A שבועה not to do a מצוה simply does not take effect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא on the משנה, connected to the משנה's rule that oaths apply to things without substance (Step 7).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A נדר takes effect on a מצוה matter just like on an optional matter. A שבועה does not.

steps.title: The oath stringency: oaths apply even to things with no substance
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes: a שבועה takes effect even on things without physical substance, which a נדר cannot do.
steps.simpleTranslation: The stringency in oaths is that oaths take effect on something with no substance just like on something with substance, which is not so with vows.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives the second half of the comparison: the area where a שבועה is stronger than a נדר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same rule the משנה taught in Steps 5 and 7. One can swear about sleeping or throwing a pebble, and that oath takes effect. A נדר cannot take effect on something like that. It matches the point in Step 4 that a שבועה, unlike the prohibitions in that list, can apply to things with no physical substance.

keyTerms.meaning: A thing with no physical substance, like an action such as sleeping

steps.whatToRemember: נדר is stronger because it takes effect on a מצוה matter. שבועה is stronger because it takes effect on something with no physical substance.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא gives the basic difference between נדרים and שבועות, and it backs up the משנה's rule about oaths on things like sleeping.

phrases.english: The stringency in oaths: that oaths take effect
on a thing that has no substance
just like on a thing that has substance,
which is not so with vows.

steps.triggerLanguage: חוֹמֶר בַּשְּׁבוּעוֹת – שֶׁהַשְּׁבוּעוֹת חָלוֹת עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַמָּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided comparison started in Step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שבועה takes effect on something with no substance just like on something with substance. A נדר does not.

steps.title: What kind of giving is meant by 'I will give'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's example of an oath to give or not to give to someone, and asks what kind of giving is meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? He said: 'On my oath, I will give to so-and-so,' or 'I will not give.' What is the case of 'I will give'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the משנה's example of an oath about the future and asks exactly what case it means. This sets up the next move, where the גמרא tries out possible answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave 'I will give to so-and-so' as an example of a שבועה that takes effect. The גמרא wants to know what is being given, because some kinds of giving are already required by the תורה, and an oath may not take effect on those.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it? / What case is meant?

phrases.english: How so?
He said: "On my oath, I will give to so-and-so,"
or: "I will not give."
What is the case of "I will give"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ברייתא about vows and oaths to explaining the משנה's examples of oaths about the future.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of giving the משנה means in an oath to give to someone.

steps.title: It cannot mean charity to a poor person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the case is צדקה to a poor person, then rejects it, because he is already under oath from הר סיני to give צדקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it means צדקה to a poor person, he is already under oath from הר סיני to give that, as it says: 'You shall surely give him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the first possible answer, צדקה to a poor person, and knocks it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A new שבועה cannot take effect on something a person is already bound to do by the תורה. Since the פסוק already commands giving to the poor, an oath to give צדקה adds nothing, so the משנה must mean a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (offers an answer that will be rejected)
Already under oath from הר סיני (already commanded by the תורה)

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean giving צדקה is unimportant. It means the opposite: the obligation is already so firm that a personal oath cannot be added on top of it.

phrases.english: If you say it means charity to a poor person,
he is already under oath from Mount Sinai,
as it is said: "You shall surely give him"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers and rejects a first answer to the question of step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects reading 'I will give' as giving צדקה to a poor person.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: An oath cannot take effect on something the person is already obligated to do from הר סיני.

steps.title: It means a gift to a rich person
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that the משנה's case is an oath to give a gift to a rich person, which is not a מצוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means a gift to a rich person.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its real answer: the oath is about giving a gift to a rich person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Giving a present to a rich person is not commanded by the תורה, so the person is fully free to choose. That is why an oath can take effect on it.
steps.whatToRemember: An oath to give only takes effect on giving that is not already a מצוה, like a gift to a rich person. An oath to give צדקה does not add a new oath, because the person is already bound from הר סיני.

phrases.english: Rather, it means a gift to a rich person.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the accepted answer after the rejection in step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה's oath 'I will give' refers to a gift to a rich person, which is optional and so can be the subject of an oath.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי יוחנן to an oath not to sleep
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's example 'I will sleep / I will not sleep' and challenges it from רבי יוחנן, who rules that an oath not to sleep for three days is punished with lashes right away and the person may sleep.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'That I will sleep' or 'that I will not sleep.' Is that really so? But רבי יוחנן said: One who says, 'On my oath, I will not sleep for three days,' they give him lashes, and he may sleep immediately!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next example from the משנה and attacks it using a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן treats an oath not to sleep for three days as impossible to keep, so it is a false oath from the start: he gets lashes and may sleep right away. If so, how can the משנה say an oath 'I will not sleep' takes effect like a normal oath?

keyTerms.meaning: Is that really so? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: "That I will sleep" or "that I will not sleep":
Is that so?!
But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
One who says: "On my oath, I will not sleep
for three days":
they give him lashes
phrases.notes: No one can stay awake three days, so it counts as a false oath the moment he says it.

phrases.english: and he may sleep immediately!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next example in the משנה and raises a challenge against it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that an oath 'I will not sleep' takes effect as a normal oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן rules that an oath not to sleep is impossible to keep and is a false oath from the start, so it should not take effect as a normal oath.

steps.title: Difference: saying 'three days' or not
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יוחנן speaks of someone who said 'three days,' while the משנה speaks of someone who did not say 'three days.'
steps.simpleTranslation: There, he said 'three days.' Here, he did not say 'three days.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by showing that the two rulings deal with different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'three days' makes the oath impossible, so it is a false oath from the start. Without 'three days,' the oath is understood to last only as long as a person can really stay awake, so it is possible and takes effect.
steps.whatToRemember: An oath not to sleep for three days is impossible, so it is a false oath. A plain oath not to sleep, without a time limit, is possible and takes effect.

phrases.english: There, he said "three" days;
here, he did not say "three" days.
phrases.notes: Without a time, his oath covers only as long as a person can really stay awake.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (אוקימתא by wording of the oath)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any oath not to sleep is impossible and therefore a false oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only an oath that names three days is impossible; an oath without a time limit is possible and takes effect.

steps.title: The stone-in-the-sea oath and a dispute about a past-tense version
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's example "I will throw a stone into the sea / I will not throw," then brings a dispute. If someone swears that another person threw, or did not throw, a stone into the sea, רב says he is חייב and שמואל says he is פטור.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: "I will throw a stone into the sea" and "I will not throw." It was stated: if someone says, "I swear that so-and-so threw a stone into the sea" or "that he did not throw," רב says he is liable and שמואל says he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא picks up the next example in the משנה, a pointless future action like throwing a stone into the sea. It then brings a new case: an oath about the past, about what someone else did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's case is about the future and about the swearer's own action. The new case changes two things: it is about the past, and it is about another person (פלוני). רב and שמואל argue whether this kind of oath still counts as a שבועת ביטוי that brings a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable. Here it means he must bring a קרבן for a false oath
Exempt, does not bring a קרבן

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. The משנה is about "I will throw" (my own future action), while רב and שמואל argue about "so-and-so threw" (someone else's past action).

phrases.english: "That I will throw a stone into the sea"
and "that I will not throw."
It was stated: "An oath that so-and-so threw a stone into the sea"
or "that he did not throw";
רב says: he is liable,
and שמואל says: he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the sleeping example (steps 17-18) to the משנה's next example, and opens a new אמוראי dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For an oath that someone else threw or did not throw a stone in the past, רב holds he is חייב and שמואל holds he is פטור.

steps.title: The reasoning of רב and שמואל
steps.stepSummary: רב makes him liable because the oath can be said in both a negative and a positive form. שמואל exempts him because this oath cannot be said about the future.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says he is liable, because this oath can be said as "no" and as "yes." שמואל says he is exempt, because it cannot be said about the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רב and שמואל rule the way they do. Each one uses a different test for which oaths count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, the test is whether the oath can go both ways, "he threw" or "he did not throw," and this one can. For שמואל, the test is whether the same oath could also be said about the future. Since you cannot swear what פלוני will do, because that is not in your hands, this oath does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: "No" and "yes," meaning a negative and a positive form
It does not exist, it does not apply

steps.whatToRemember: רב: an oath counts if it can be said as yes or no. שמואל: it must also be something you could swear about the future.

phrases.english: רב says he is liable –
because it can be said in "no" and "yes."
And שמואל says he is exempt –
because it cannot be said about the future.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind the two rulings stated in step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's test is לאו והן (both forms possible). שמואל's test is whether it could apply להבא (to the future).

steps.title: Is this the same as the dispute of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether רב and שמואל are really repeating the older מחלוקת between רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא. It quotes the משנה where רבי ישמעאל says one is liable only for oaths about the future, based on the פסוק "להרע או להיטיב."
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about the same thing as רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא? As we learned: רבי ישמעאל says one is liable only for something in the future, because it says "to do bad or to do good."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests that רב and שמואל may simply be following the two sides of an earlier תנאים dispute. It begins quoting that dispute so we can compare.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל learns from "להרע או להיטיב" that a שבועת ביטוי is only about the future, since you can only "do" bad or good from now on. שמואל's focus on the future sounds similar, so the גמרא wonders if the אמוראים are just repeating the תנאים. This is only a suggestion (לימא), not a conclusion.

keyTerms.meaning: "Shall we say?" This offers a suggestion the גמרא will test
The future, what is still to come
"To do bad or to do good," words from the פסוק of שבועת ביטוי

steps.confusionAlert: A "לימא" question is a trial suggestion. The גמרא often ends up rejecting it, so do not treat it as the final answer.

phrases.aramaic: לֵימָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
phrases.english: Shall we say that in the dispute of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא
they are disagreeing?
As we learned: רבי ישמעאל says:

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא עַל הֶעָתִיד לָבֹא,
phrases.english: one is liable only for what is in the future,
as it is said: "to do bad or to do good."

steps.triggerLanguage: לֵימָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא קָא מִיפַּלְגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests whether the רב/שמואל dispute from steps 19-20 is simply the older תנאים dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב and שמואל are just following the two sides of רבי ישמעאל and רבי עקיבא.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא challenges רבי ישמעאל's reading of the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא argues that if we read "להרע או להיטיב" strictly, it would only cover oaths about doing bad or good. Then where would we learn oaths about things that have nothing to do with bad or good?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to him: If so, I only know about things that involve doing bad or good. Where do I learn about things that do not involve doing bad or good?
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the quoted משנה, רבי עקיבא attacks רבי ישמעאל's way of reading the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל limited the oath to the future because of the words "to do bad or good." רבי עקיבא points out that if we take those words that literally, oaths about neutral things would be left out too. Yet everyone agrees those neutral oaths count, like throwing a stone into the sea.

keyTerms.meaning: "If so," meaning if your reading is right
"From where?" meaning what is the source

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: אִם כֵּן,
phrases.english: רבי עקיבא said to him: If so,

phrases.aramaic: אֵין לִי אֶלָּא דְּבָרִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶן הֲרָעָה וַהֲטָבָה,
phrases.english: I only have things that involve doing bad and doing good;

phrases.aramaic: דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶן הֲרָעָה וַהֲטָבָה מִנַּיִן?
phrases.english: things that do not involve doing bad and doing good, from where?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא: אִם כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the משנה: רבי עקיבא challenges the source רבי ישמעאל used in step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's strict reading of "להרע או להיטיב"
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A strict reading would also leave out neutral oaths, which are surely included, so the words cannot be read that narrowly.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל: neutral oaths come from an extra word in the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל answers that oaths about neutral things are learned from a ריבוי, an extra word in the פסוק that widens the law.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: From the widening of the פסוק.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ישמעאל defends himself. He says neutral oaths are included because the פסוק adds them through a widening word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל keeps his reading that "להרע או להיטיב" points to the future. He explains that neutral matters are added by a separate ריבוי in the פסוק, not by these words.

keyTerms.meaning: A widening in the פסוק, where extra wording includes more cases

phrases.english: He said to him: From the widening of the verse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי עקיבא's question from step 22.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a separate source (a ריבוי) for the case that was asked about
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Reading "להרע או להיטיב" strictly would leave out neutral oaths.
steps.terutzMaskana: Neutral oaths are included through a ריבוי in the פסוק, while the future-only limit still stands.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא: if the פסוק widens for one thing, it widens for the other
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers back: if the ריבוי can widen the law to neutral matters, it can just as well widen it to oaths about the past.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If the פסוק widened for this, the פסוק widened for that!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא turns רבי ישמעאל's own answer against him. The ריבוי that includes neutral oaths should also include oaths about the past.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once רבי ישמעאל admits the פסוק includes more than its plain words, רבי עקיבא says there is no reason to stop at neutral matters. The same widening covers past oaths too, so for רבי עקיבא one can be liable for an oath about the past.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the heart of the תנאים dispute: רבי עקיבא holds past oaths count, and רבי ישמעאל limits them to the future. The גמרא wants to see whether רב and שמואל line up with these two sides.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: אִם רִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב לְכָךְ,
phrases.english: He said to him: If the verse widened for this,
phrases.notes: "This" means the neutral matters רבי ישמעאל just mentioned.

phrases.english: the verse widened for that!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אִם רִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב לְכָךְ, רִיבָּה הַכָּתוּב לְכָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי עקיבא answers back against רבי ישמעאל's answer in step 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ישמעאל's use of the ריבוי only for neutral matters
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the ריבוי reaches past the plain words, nothing stops it from also including oaths about the past.

steps.title: The suggestion: רב follows רבי עקיבא, שמואל follows רבי ישמעאל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא completes its proposal that רב holds like רבי עקיבא and שמואל holds like רבי ישמעאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that רב follows רבי עקיבא, and שמואל follows רבי ישמעאל?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the question it opened in Step 21. It suggests that the argument between רב and שמואל is really the old argument between רבי עקיבא and רבי ישמעאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא makes a person liable for oaths about the past, so he would fit רב, who makes him liable. רבי ישמעאל says one is liable only for oaths about the future, so he would fit שמואל, who exempts him.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with the view of רבי עקיבא

phrases.english: Rav, who said [he is liable], holds like Rabbi Akiva,
phrases.notes: This finishes the question that started in Step 21: shall we say that...

phrases.english: and Shmuel, who said [he is exempt], holds like Rabbi Yishmael?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, וּשְׁמוּאֵל דְּאָמַר כְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the suggestion opened in Step 21, now that the background מחלוקת (Steps 21-24) has been laid out.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the dispute between רב and שמואל simply the same as the dispute between רבי עקיבא and רבי ישמעאל about oaths on the past?

steps.title: No: according to רבי ישמעאל everyone agrees there is no liability
steps.stepSummary: Under רבי ישמעאל, even רב would agree he is exempt. If an oath about one's own past action is exempt, an oath about someone else's action certainly is.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי ישמעאל, everyone agrees. If רבי ישמעאל does not make him liable for a past oath about something that could also be sworn about the future, is it even a question that he is exempt for something that cannot be sworn about the future at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Under רבי ישמעאל's view, there would be nothing for רב and שמואל to argue about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ישמעאל exempts even a past oath like 'I threw a stone,' which could also be sworn about the future ('I will throw'). An oath that another person threw a stone cannot be sworn about the future at all, since he does not control it. So it is a קל וחומר that רבי ישמעאל exempts it, and רב could not argue on that.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it even a question? (it is obvious)

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Yishmael –
everyone agrees [that he is exempt];
now, a matter that can exist [as an oath] about the future,

phrases.aramaic: לָא מְחַיַּיב עֲלַהּ רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל לְשֶׁעָבַר,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael does not make him liable for it about the past,
a matter that cannot exist about the future, is it even a question?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל – כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of Step 25 by showing that רב could not hold like רבי ישמעאל.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the suggestion from Step 25 that the רב/שמואל dispute lines up with the רבי עקיבא/רבי ישמעאל dispute. Under רבי ישמעאל there would be nothing to argue about.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Under רבי ישמעאל, even רב would have to agree to exempt him, by a קל וחומר. So the dispute cannot line up with רבי עקיבא versus רבי ישמעאל.

steps.title: The real dispute is how to understand רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: רב and שמואל both follow רבי עקיבא. רב applies his view fully, while שמואל limits it to oaths that could also be about the future.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they argue, it is within the view of רבי עקיבא. רב follows רבי עקיבא plainly. שמואל says: רבי עקיבא makes one liable for a past oath only when it could also be said about the future. But for something that cannot be said about the future, he does not make him liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what רב and שמואל really argue about. Both accept רבי עקיבא, but they disagree about how far his view goes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, רבי עקיבא's liability for past oaths covers every past oath, even about someone else's action. שמואל says רבי עקיבא only includes past oaths of a kind that could also exist about the future, like 'I threw.' This matches שמואל's reason in Step 20: this oath cannot be said about the future.

keyTerms.meaning: When they do argue / where their argument really is
Only up to here; X said it only in this case

steps.whatToRemember: רב and שמואל both hold like רבי עקיבא. רב applies 'liable for the past' to every oath. שמואל applies it only to oaths that could also have been sworn about the future.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common move in the גמרא: two אמוראים are not repeating a תנאים argument. They are arguing about how far one תנא's view reaches.

phrases.english: When they argue – it is according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rav – holds like Rabbi Akiva [with no limit];
and Shmuel says:

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא מְחַיֵּיב רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva makes him liable only
there, about the past,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the משנה quoted in Steps 22-24, where רבי עקיבא makes past oaths liable.

phrases.english: but a matter that can exist about the future –
Rabbi Akiva makes him liable [even] about the past;
but a thing that cannot exist about the future – no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the suggestion in Step 26, the גמרא gives the correct way to place רב and שמואל.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The dispute is not רבי עקיבא against רבי ישמעאל. It is about how far רבי עקיבא's view goes: fully (רב), or only for oaths that could also be about the future (שמואל).

steps.title: Opening a new suggestion: shall we say it is a dispute?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a new attempt to tie רב and שמואל to an earlier dispute.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say that this is like a dispute...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is starting a new suggestion, and the rest continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having placed רב and שמואל inside רבי עקיבא's view, the גמרא now looks for another earlier dispute that might match their argument. The details come next.

phrases.english: Shall we say [that it is] in the dispute

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new attempt to connect the רב and שמואל dispute to an earlier dispute.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the רב and שמואל dispute match another earlier dispute? The text continues on the next amud.
